Every time [Moose](https://github.com/moosetechnology) evolves, the tools built on top of it have to evolve as well. So this summer, during my Mitacs Globalink internship at ÉTS Montréal under the supervision of Professor Christopher Fuhrman, I migrated the [FamixTypeScript](https://github.com/fuhrmanator/FamixTypeScript) metamodel and updated its companion importer [`ts2famix`](https://github.com/fuhrmanator/FamixTypeScriptImporter) to the latest version, Moose 13, while also setting up a CI/CD pipeline in Github Actions that automates tests across both environments, providing end-to-end validation for the changes.

## Assumptions

This post assumes familiarity with [`ts2famix`](../typescript-in-moose/), and a basic understanding of the two techstacks involved: TypeScript and Pharo Smalltalk/Moose. The modeling of generics and concretizations builds on the work described in Clotilde Toullec's post [Parametrics next generation](https://modularmoose.org/blog/2025-05-07-parametrics-next-generation/).

## Automating End-To-End Testing

`ts2famix` consists of two steps. First, we use the importer to parse the project and create a model.json. This file is then loaded into the Pharo environment with FamixTypeScript metamodel used to represent the project.

Previously, both these steps were tested independently. The importer was tested using jest, while the Pharo tests were run manually when importing the model into the moose environment. Although both steps were working independently, this did not guarantee that the model generated could be successfully imported into Pharo or that it contained all the expected entities. Discrepencies between the importer and metamodel might go undetected.

To address this, I implemented a CI/CD pipeline in Github Actions that automates testing across both environments. Whenever new code is pushed to the repository, the CI/CD kicks in and the follows steps occur:

1. **Run the Jest test suite:** The importer’s Jest tests verify that different aspects of TypeScript syntax are correctly captured in the generated model.

2. **Generate a sample project:** The pipeline combines the code snippets tested in the test files into a sample project.

3. **Generate the model:** The importer processes this sample project and generates a `model.json` file.

4. **Import the model into Pharo:** The generated model is loaded into the Pharo environment containing the FamixTypeScript metamodel.

5. **Run the Pharo tests:** The Pharo test suite validates that the expected entities are successfully imported into the model.

![End-to-end testing pipeline](ci-cd.png){.lightbox}

## Migrating FamixTypeScript metamodel and ts2famix Importer to Moose 13.

`FamixTypeScript` is build on top of Moose ecosystem. When Moose was updated from version 12 to 13, changes in the foundational moose entities meant that the existing metamodel is not compatible with the new version. For this reason, FamixTypeScript metamodel and subsequently, the importer, had to be updated for the new version.

### Introducing Entity Typing

Moose 13 introduced `EntityTyping`, an association that replaced the direct relationship between a typed entity and its type. This change made type relationships more in line with the lastest moose structure and gave a more flexible way to represent TypeScript types.

The new structure is shown in the following diagram:

![Entity Typing Structure from [Parametrics: Next Generation](https://modularmoose.org/blog/2025-05-07-parametrics-next-generation/#entity-typing)](https://modularmoose.org/_astro/uml-entity-typing.DDPWOCX4_Z1xnFi4.webp){.lightbox}

The following FamixTypeScript entities were updated to use the new `EntityTyping` structure:

- `Function`
- `ParametricFunction`
- `ArrowFunction`
- `ParametricArrowFunction`
- `Method`
- `Accessor`
- `ParametricMethod`
- `EnumValue`
- `Parameter`
- `Property`
- `Variable`

### Restructuring Concretizations

In object-oriented programming, generic entities can be declared using type parameters and then used with specific types. For example, consider the following TypeScript code:

```typescript
class Box<T> {
    value: T;
}

const box = new Box<string>();
```

Here, `Box` is a generic class with a type parameter `T`. When `Box<string>` is instantiated, `T` is associated with the concrete type `string`.

The Famix model needs to represent both the generic entity and its usages seperately. Previously, representing a concretization involved creating a duplicate of the generic entity and linking the duplicate directly to the original. The updated Moose metamodel introduces a dedicated `Concretization` entity to represent this relationship explicitly.

A concretization is modeled as a three-way association connecting the generic entity, the concrete type, and the kind of concretization being performed.

The diagram below illustrates the new structure.

![Concretization Structure from [Parametrics: Next Generation](https://modularmoose.org/blog/2025-05-07-parametrics-next-generation/#parametric-associations)](https://modularmoose.org/_astro/uml-parametric-association.fXCQF5U9_6Lk40.webp){.lightbox}

### Parametric Associations

Alongside with the changes to concretizations, the new metamodel introducted 5 parametric associations. These associations specifically represent relationships involving generic entities being instantiated by a concrete types.

#### Parametric Implementation

Parametric implementation represents a class implementing a generic interface. For example:

```typescript
interface Repository<T> {}

class UserRepository implements Repository<string> {}
```

Here, `UserRepository` implements `Repository<string>`.

#### Parametric Inheritance

Parametric inheritance represents inheritance with a generic type. For example:

```typescript
class Animal<T> {}

class Dog extends Animal<string> {}
```

Here, `Dog` inherits from the concretized type `Animal<string>`.

#### Parametric Invocation

Parametric invocation represents a call to a generic function or method with concrete type arguments. For example:

```typescript
function identity<T>(value: T): T {
    return value;
}

identity<number>(42);
```

Here, the invocation supplies `number` as the type argument for `T`.

#### Parametric Reference

A parametric reference occurs when a generic entity is used in other places in code. For example:

```typescript
class Box<T> {
  value!: T;
}

function createStringBox() {
  const StringBox = Box<string>;
}
```

Here, the function `createStringBox` refers to the generic class `Box` with the type argument `string`. The concretization maps the type parameter `T` to `string`.

#### Parametric Entity Typing

Parametric entity typing represents a typing relationship involving a parameterized type, extending the `EntityTyping` association with support for concretizations.

For example:

```typescript
class Box<T> {
    value: T;
}

let box: Box<string>;
```

Here, entity typing binds the generic type parameter `T` to the concrete type `string` while declaring the Type of the Entity as `Box<string>`

![Parameterized Associations Structure from [Parametrics: Next Generation](https://modularmoose.org/blog/2025-05-07-parametrics-next-generation/#summary)](https://modularmoose.org/_astro/uml-new-parametrics-mm.BTiU1iMv_1BpMeh.webp){.lightbox}

### Progress in the Importer and npm Release

All of the associations discussed above have been incorporated into the metamodel, and their APIs have been added to the importer. Among these, Entity Typing, Parametric Entity Typing, Parametric Invocation, and Parametric Inheritance are implemented in the importer's logic and are now visible in the generated model.

Parametric Reference has not been implemented yet. It is built on Reference, which is not yet handled in the parsing logic. The parametric conterpart would be added after References are in place.

Parametric Implementation is also not implemented. The importer currently treats implementation and extension as the same kind of relationship. After discussing this with Professor Fuhrman, we concluded that the two may be too similar in TypeScript to need separate associations. Currently it is handled through inheritance.

In line to these changes, many of the tests inside the importer as well as inside the metamodel have been updated to reflect the new structures. A new version of `ts2famix` including these changes have been published on npm. The latest version at the time of writing is [v3.3.0](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ts2famix).

## Adding TSX Support and Planning a TypeScript Famix Extension

Another goal of my project was to add `TSX` support to the importer. `ts2famix` is built on top of [`ts-morph`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ts-morph), and while experimenting with it, support for TSX syntax was found. This meant that ts2famix can be extended to support TSX syntax using the same tools the importer is built on.

Initially, we planned to incorporate the TSX extention into the `FamixTypeScript` metamodel itself. After furthur discussions, we concluded that a seperate metamodel built on top of `FamixTypeScript` might be a better approach. A draft of the metamodel, covering the entities specific to TSX, have been modeled and are shown below:

![Proposed TSX Structure](tsx-metamodel-structure.png){.lightbox}

### TSX Entities

Each entity described in the TSX metamodel corresponds to a JSX node inside `ts-morph`. They are described below, from more general ones to more specific.

#### FamixTSXEntity

`FamixTSXEntity` is the root of the TSX metamodel. It extends `FamixBaseElement`, so every TSX entity fits into the existing Famix infrastructure. It is never created directly, it only provides a base for all entities below.

#### FamixTSXContainer

`FamixTSXContainer` is an abstract entity for those TSX entities that can contain other TSX entities.

#### FamixTSXElement

`FamixTSXElement` represents a JSX element with an opening and a closing tag. It can contain text, expressions, and other elements as children.

```jsx
<div className="card">
  <h1>Title</h1>
</div>
```

Here, both `<div>` and `<h1>` are `FamixTSXElement`.

#### FamixTSXFragment

`FamixTSXFragment` represents a JSX fragment, which acts as placeholder to group children without adding an extra element to the output.

```jsx
<>
  <h1>Title</h1>
</>
```

The `<>...</>` wrapper is a `FamixTSXFragment`.

#### FamixTSXExpression

`FamixTSXExpression` represents a JavaScript expression inside JSX between curly braces.

```jsx
<ul>
  {items.map(item => <li>{item.name}</li>)}
</ul>
```

Both `{items.map(...)}` and `{item.name}` are `FamixTSXExpression`.

#### FamixTSXText

`FamixTSXText` represents the plain text between JSX tags.

```jsx
<p>Hello, world!</p>
```

The text `Hello, world!` is a `FamixTSXText`.

#### FamixTSXSelfClosingElement

`FamixTSXSelfClosingElement` represents a JSX element that closes itself and has no children.

```jsx
<img src="logo.png" />
<UserCard user={user} />
```

Both `<img />` and `<UserCard />` are `FamixTSXSelfClosingElement`.

#### FamixTSXAttribute

`FamixTSXAttribute` represents a single named attribute (also called prop) on a JSX element. Its value can be a string literal or an expression.

```jsx
<button type="submit" onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>
```

Here, `type="submit"` and `onClick={handleClick}` are both `FamixTSXAttribute` of the `<button>` element.

#### FamixTSXSpreadAttribute

`FamixTSXSpreadAttribute` are a spread of an object's properties as attributes. It is still an attribute but its purpose is to apply many attributes at once.

```jsx
<Input {...inputProps} disabled />
```

Here, `{...inputProps}` is an `FamixTSXSpreadAttribute`.

Following is a table mapping the TSX Entites to their tsmporph counterpart.

| Famix TSX entity | ts-morph counterpart |
|---|---|
| `FamixTSXEntity` | No direct counterpart |
| `FamixTSXContainer` | No direct counterpart |
| `FamixTSXElement` | `JsxElement` |
| `FamixTSXSelfClosingElement` | `JsxSelfClosingElement` |
| `FamixTSXFragment` | `JsxFragment` |
| `FamixTSXExpression` | `JsxExpression` |
| `FamixTSXText` | `JsxText` |
| `FamixTSXAttribute` | `JsxAttribute` |
| `FamixTSXSpreadAttribute` | `JsxSpreadAttribute` |

Right now the importer is able to accept `.tsx` files, but capturing TSX specific entities are yet to be added into the importer.

## AI Assistance

AI tools were valuable throughout this project. The biggest challenge faced during development was the addition of the new concretization structure. This change touched many different entities and many parts of the codebase. With the help of AI, I was able to determine and implement the scope of this change. In this case, it helped me implement these changes at a quicker pace.

AI immensely helped me understand the structure of the metamodel and the importer's parsing logic. This understanding helped me to implement Parametric Associations and the Entity Typing changes. AI made certain tasks such as repetitive changes and large refactors easier, while the design decisions and much of the implementations were my own.

## Where to Go From Here

There are lots of different directions this project could take. The most immediate would be to complete the parametric associations and their related entities, starting with References, on which Parametric Reference depends. After that, a separate Pharo metamodel for TSX, built on top of `FamixTypeScript`, can be created and integrated into the importer. The Moose post on [connecting and extending metamodels](https://modularmoose.org/blog/2021-05-15-connecting-meta-models/) could be of great help for this. Finally, the importer itself could benefit from a refactor. The `EntityDictionary` has many separate maps for different kinds of entities, several of which are rarely used. A redesign of these global maps to better serve the parser logic would be a great step in making the importer easier to maintain in the future.
